name: Nimzo-Indian: Sämisch
summary: The Sämisch Variation (4.a3) forces ...Bxc3+ bxc3, handing White doubled c-pawns and a broad centre with the bishop pair against Black's structural pressure.
intro: The Sämisch Variation is White's most uncompromising answer to the Nimzo-Indian, playing 4.a3 to force the immediate exchange 4...Bxc3+ 5.bxc3. White voluntarily accepts doubled c-pawns in return for the bishop pair and a broad pawn centre, pawns on c3 and d4 that can be reinforced by f3 and e4, promising a powerful space advantage and attacking chances. Black's counterplay is aimed squarely at that structure: with ...c5, ...d5, ...Nc6, ...b6 and ...Ba6, Black blockades the centre, pressures the weak doubled c-pawns, and tries to prove that White's ambitious pawns are more target than strength. The traditional main battleground runs 5...c5 6.f3 d5, when both sides' plans collide head-on.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nc3 Bb4 a3 Bxc3+ bxc3 c5 f3 d5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Sämisch is a classic clash of static weakness against a dynamic centre. White's doubled c-pawns on c3 and c4 are a long-term liability, and the c4-pawn in particular can become chronically weak, so Black aims to fix and besiege it with ...c5, ...Nc6, ...Na5 and the manoeuvre ...b6 and ...Ba6 hitting c4 from the side. In compensation White gains the two bishops and a mobile pawn mass; the plan of f3 and e4 builds an imposing centre, and if White achieves e4 and d5 the bishops and space can generate a dangerous kingside attack. The whole variation asks whether White's centre will roll forward or be blockaded and left with weak pawns.

Piece placement is sharply defined by the pawn tension. White develops the dark-squared bishop to d3 or e2 and the king's knight often to e2 rather than blocking the f3-pawn on f3, castles short, and prepares e4; the light-squared bishop and rooks support the central break. Black castles, plays ...d5 to challenge c4, and directs the knights toward the weak c4-pawn and the blockading squares, while the queen and rooks pile onto the c-file and the c4 target. If the centre stays fixed, Black's positional pressure on the doubled pawns dominates; if White breaks with e4 and opens lines, the initiative and bishops can overwhelm Black. Precise timing of the central breaks decides which scenario prevails.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: After 5.bxc3 the principal line is 5...c5 6.f3, preparing e4, when 6...d5 is the traditional main move, striking at c4 and the centre before White is ready. Play can continue 7.cxd5 Nxd5 or 7...exd5, and 8.dxc5 leads to sharp, concrete positions, while White can also maintain the tension and build up slowly toward e4. A major alternative is the plan with ...Nc6, ...b6 and ...Ba6, sometimes preceded by ...O-O and ...d6, which keeps the centre closed and concentrates purely on winning the c4-pawn.

Black is not obliged to enter the ...c5 and ...d5 main line: setups with an early ...d6 and ...Nc6 followed by ...e5, or ...b6 and ...Ba6 to pressure c4 without fixing the centre, are fully respectable and steer play into slower positional channels. White, in turn, can delay f3 in favour of quick development with e3, Bd3 and Ne2, preparing e4 a move later, or castle first and choose the moment for the central push. Because both sides have clear, opposing plans, White's centre and bishops against Black's blockade and pressure on c4, the Sämisch produces some of the most double-edged strategic fighting in the whole Nimzo-Indian.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation bears the name of Friedrich Sämisch, the German grandmaster of the early twentieth century, who pioneered the direct 4.a3 approach and lent his name to sharp, space-grabbing systems in several openings, including the Sämisch Variation of the King's Indian Defence. It became a major weapon in mid-twentieth-century practice, prized for the way White's central pawn majority and bishop pair could be turned against a static structure, and Sämisch positions supplied many model games in the handling of doubled pawns and central pawn mobility.

Although later theory found reliable methods for Black to blockade and target the c-pawns, blunting some of White's early enthusiasm, the line retains its reputation as a principled, aggressive try. It is still chosen when White wants a maximal, fighting game against the Nimzo-Indian, trading structural soundness for the two bishops and the chance of a rolling central attack.
